name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q01 - Peak magnetic field from electric field amplitude

questiontext.text: A plane electromagnetic wave propagates in vacuum. At a given point, the amplitude of the oscillating electric field is \(E_0 = 90\text{ V/m}\). What is the amplitude of the oscillating magnetic field \(B_0\) at this point? (Take the speed of light in vacuum \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Electric field amplitude: \(E_0 = 90\text{ V/m}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
In a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum, the peak amplitudes of the coupled electric and magnetic fields are related by the wave velocity.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into the formula:
\[B_0 = \frac{90\text{ V/m}}{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} = 3.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The unit is \(\text{V}\cdot\text{s}/\text{m}^2 = \text{Tesla (T)}\). The computed magnetic field amplitude is \(3.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The amplitude of the oscillating magnetic field is \(3.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q02 - Wavelength calculation in frequency modulated radio band

questiontext.text: An FM radio station broadcasts electromagnetic waves at a carrier frequency of \(100\text{ MHz}\). What is the wavelength of these radio waves in vacuum? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Carrier frequency: \(\nu = 100\text{ MHz} = 100 \times 10^6\text{ Hz} = 1.0 \times 10^8\text{ s}^{-1}\).
Propagation speed in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Radio waves are electromagnetic waves that propagate at the speed of light in vacuum.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[c = \nu \lambda \implies \lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[\lambda = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{1.0 \times 10^8\text{ s}^{-1}} = 3.0\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The wavelength is \(3.0\text{ m}\), which is consistent with the standard VHF radio band.

Final Conceptual Answer:
The wavelength of the radio waves is \(3.0\text{ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q03 - Frequency determination from visible light wavelength

questiontext.text: A beam of red light has a wavelength of \(\lambda = 600\text{ nm}\) in vacuum. What is the oscillation frequency of this electromagnetic wave? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Wavelength: \(\lambda = 600\text{ nm} = 600 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m} = 6.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Visible light consists of electromagnetic waves governed by the universal wave speed equation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\nu = \frac{c}{\lambda}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\nu = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{6.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}} = 0.50 \times 10^{15}\text{ Hz} = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The optical frequency of \(5.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\) falls squarely within the visible range (\(4 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\) to \(7 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\)).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The oscillation frequency is \(5.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q04 - Angular frequency from electromagnetic wave frequency

questiontext.text: A plane electromagnetic wave travelling in free space has a frequency of \(\nu = 25\text{ MHz}\). What is the angular frequency \(\omega\) of this wave? (Use \(\pi = 3.14\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Frequency: \(\nu = 25\text{ MHz} = 2.5 \times 10^7\text{ Hz}\).
Constant: \(\pi = 3.14\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The angular frequency \(\omega\) describes the radian rate of phase variation per unit time.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\omega = 2\pi \nu\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\omega = 2 \times 3.14 \times (2.5 \times 10^7\text{ s}^{-1}) = 6.28 \times 2.5 \times 10^7\text{ rad/s} = 1.57 \times 10^8\text{ rad/s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{rad/s}\). The computed angular frequency is \(1.57 \times 10^8\text{ rad/s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The angular frequency is \(1.57 \times 10^8\text{ rad/s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q05 - Displacement current from charging rate of capacitor

questiontext.text: During the charging of a capacitor, the charge on its plates increases at a constant rate of \(0.40\text{ C/s}\). What is the instantaneous displacement current across the region between the plates?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Rate of increase of plate charge: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0.40\text{ C/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Electric flux between parallel plates of area \(A\) is \(\Phi_E = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\). Maxwell's displacement current is \(i_d = \varepsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[i_d = \varepsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}\right) = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[i_d = 0.40\text{ C/s} = 0.40\text{ A}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
By current continuity, the displacement current equals the rate of change of charge on the plates, \(0.40\text{ A}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The displacement current is \(0.40\text{ A}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q06 - Wave propagation number from microwave wavelength

questiontext.text: A microwave has a wavelength of \(\lambda = 3.0\text{ cm}\) in free space. What is the magnitude of its propagation wave vector \(k\)? (Use \(\pi = 3.1416\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Wavelength: \(\lambda = 3.0\text{ cm} = 0.030\text{ m}\).
Constant: \(\pi = 3.1416\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The wave vector magnitude (wave number) \(k\) is related to wavelength by the spatial radian rate.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[k = \frac{2 \times 3.1416}{0.030\text{ m}} = \frac{6.2832}{0.030} \approx 209.4\text{ rad/m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{rad/m}\). The wave number is \(209.4\text{ rad/m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The magnitude of the wave vector is \(209.4\text{ rad/m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q07 - Electric amplitude from small magnetic amplitude

questiontext.text: The magnetic field amplitude of an electromagnetic wave travelling in free space is \(B_0 = 2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ T}\). What is the electric field amplitude \(E_0\) of the wave? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Magnetic field amplitude: \(B_0 = 2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ T}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
For an electromagnetic wave in free space, the electric field amplitude is directly proportional to the magnetic field amplitude.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_0 = c B_0\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E_0 = (3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}) \times (2.0 \times 10^{-8}\text{ T}) = 6.0\text{ V/m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{V/m}\). The electric field amplitude is \(6.0\text{ V/m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The electric field amplitude is \(6.0\text{ V/m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q08 - Rate of electric flux change in capacitor

questiontext.text: A conduction current of \(0.885\text{ A}\) flows into a parallel plate capacitor during charging. What is the time rate of change of electric flux \(\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t}\) between the plates? (Take \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Conduction current: \(i_c = 0.885\text{ A}\).
Permittivity of free space: \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Inside the capacitor, the current is purely displacement current: \(i_d = i_c = 0.885\text{ A}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[i_d = \varepsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t} \implies \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{i_d}{\varepsilon_0}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values:
\[\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{0.885\text{ A}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}} = 1.0 \times 10^{11}\text{ V}\cdot\text{m/s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{A}/(\text{C}^2/(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2)) = \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/(\text{C}\cdot\text{s}) = \text{V}\cdot\text{m/s}\). The rate of flux change is \(1.0 \times 10^{11}\text{ V}\cdot\text{m/s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The rate of change of electric flux is \(1.0 \times 10^{11}\text{ V}\cdot\text{m/s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q09 - Voltage slew rate across charging capacitor

questiontext.text: A capacitor of capacitance \(C = 20\text{ pF}\) is charged by a constant current of \(0.05\text{ A}\). At what rate does the potential difference \(V\) across the capacitor increase?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance: \(C = 20\text{ pF} = 20 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F}\).
Charging current: \(i = 0.05\text{ A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The charge on the capacitor is related to the potential difference by \(Q = C V\). Since \(C\) is constant, differentiating yields \(i = C \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{i}{C}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{0.05\text{ A}}{20 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F}} = \frac{5.0 \times 10^{-2}}{2.0 \times 10^{-11}} = 2.5 \times 10^9\text{ V/s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{A/F} = \text{V/s}\). The rate of potential difference increase is \(2.5 \times 10^9\text{ V/s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The potential difference increases at a rate of \(2.5 \times 10^9\text{ V/s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q10 - Electric field amplitude from magnetic field amplitude

questiontext.text: The magnetic field part of a harmonic electromagnetic wave in vacuum has an amplitude of \(B_0 = 320\text{ nT}\). What is the amplitude of the electric field part of the wave? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Magnetic field amplitude: \(B_0 = 320\text{ nT} = 3.20 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
In a plane electromagnetic wave, peak fields obey \(E_0 = c B_0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_0 = c B_0\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E_0 = (3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}) \times (3.20 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}) = 96\text{ V/m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{m/s} \times \text{T} = \text{V/m}\). The electric field amplitude is \(96\text{ V/m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The electric field amplitude is \(96\text{ V/m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q11 - Wave vector from plane wave frequency

questiontext.text: A plane electromagnetic wave propagates in free space with a frequency of \(\nu = 60.0\text{ MHz}\). What is the propagation wave number \(k\) of this wave? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\) and \(\pi = 3.142\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Frequency: \(\nu = 60.0\text{ MHz} = 6.0 \times 10^7\text{ Hz}\).
Speed of light: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
Constant: \(\pi = 3.142\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The wavelength is \(\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}\), and the wave number is \(k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \frac{2\pi\nu}{c}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}\]\[k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate wavelength:
\[\lambda = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{6.0 \times 10^7\text{ s}^{-1}} = 5.0\text{ m}\]
Calculate wave number:
\[k = \frac{2 \times 3.142}{5.0\text{ m}} = \frac{6.284}{5.0} \approx 1.26\text{ rad/m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{rad/m}\). The wave number is \(1.26\text{ rad/m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The wave number is \(1.26\text{ rad/m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q12 - Difference in wavelengths for tuning frequency band

questiontext.text: A radio receiver can tune in to any station in the frequency band from \(7.5\text{ MHz}\) to \(12.0\text{ MHz}\). What is the difference between the maximum and minimum wavelengths of this band in vacuum? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Minimum frequency: \(\nu_1 = 7.5\text{ MHz} = 7.5 \times 10^6\text{ Hz}\).
Maximum frequency: \(\nu_2 = 12.0\text{ MHz} = 1.20 \times 10^7\text{ Hz}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The wavelength corresponding to each frequency is given by \(\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\lambda_{\text{max}} = \frac{c}{\nu_1}, \quad \lambda_{\text{min}} = \frac{c}{\nu_2}, \quad \Delta \lambda = \lambda_{\text{max}} - \lambda_{\text{min}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\lambda_{\text{max}} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{7.5 \times 10^6\text{ s}^{-1}} = 40.0\text{ m}\]
\[\lambda_{\text{min}} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{12.0 \times 10^6\text{ s}^{-1}} = 25.0\text{ m}\]
\[\Delta \lambda = 40.0\text{ m} - 25.0\text{ m} = 15.0\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The wavelength range spans from \(25.0\text{ m}\) to \(40.0\text{ m}\), giving a difference of \(15.0\text{ m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The difference between maximum and minimum wavelengths is \(15.0\text{ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q13 - Magnetic amplitude and wavelength from electric amplitude

questiontext.text: A plane harmonic electromagnetic wave has an electric field amplitude \(E_0 = 120\text{ N/C}\) and a frequency \(\nu = 50.0\text{ MHz}\) in vacuum. What are the amplitude of its magnetic field \(B_0\) and its wavelength \(\lambda\)? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Electric field amplitude: \(E_0 = 120\text{ N/C} = 120\text{ V/m}\).
Frequency: \(\nu = 50.0\text{ MHz} = 5.0 \times 10^7\text{ Hz}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
In vacuum, field amplitudes and wave parameters obey \(B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c}\) and \(\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c}\]\[\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(B_0\):
\[B_0 = \frac{120\text{ V/m}}{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} = 4.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\]
Calculate \(\lambda\):
\[\lambda = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{5.0 \times 10^7\text{ s}^{-1}} = 6.0\text{ m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(B_0 = 4.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\) and \(\lambda = 6.0\text{ m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The magnetic field amplitude is \(4.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\) and the wavelength is \(6.0\text{ m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q14 - Average electric energy density calculation

questiontext.text: In a plane electromagnetic wave propagating in free space, the electric field amplitude is \(E_0 = 48\text{ V/m}\). What is the time-averaged electric energy density \(u_E\) of this wave? (Take \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Peak electric field: \(E_0 = 48\text{ V/m}\).
Permittivity of free space: \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The instantaneous electric energy density is \(u_E(t) = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E(t)^2\). For a sinusoidal wave, the time average of \(\sin^2(kz - \omega t)\) over a full cycle is \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[u_E = \frac{1}{4}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E_0^2 = (48)^2 = 2304\text{ V}^2/\text{m}^2\]
\[u_E = \frac{1}{4} \times (8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}) \times 2304 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 576 \approx 5.10 \times 10^{-9}\text{ J/m}^3\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{J/m}^3\). The computed average electric energy density is \(5.10 \times 10^{-9}\text{ J/m}^3\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The time-averaged electric energy density is \(5.10 \times 10^{-9}\text{ J/m}^3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q15 - Propagation speed in nonmagnetic dielectric medium

questiontext.text: An electromagnetic wave travels through a non-magnetic medium (\(\mu_r = 1.0\)) having a relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of \(\varepsilon_r = 2.25\). What is the phase velocity of the wave in this medium? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Relative permittivity: \(\varepsilon_r = 2.25\).
Relative permeability: \(\mu_r = 1.0\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The refractive index of a non-magnetic medium is \(n = \sqrt{\varepsilon_r \mu_r} = \sqrt{\varepsilon_r}\). The wave speed in the medium is \(v = \frac{c}{n}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_r \varepsilon_r}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\sqrt{\varepsilon_r} = \sqrt{2.25} = 1.50\]
\[v = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{1.50} = 2.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since \(\varepsilon_r > 1\), \(v < c\). The wave speed is \(2.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The speed of the wave in the medium is \(2.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q16 - Wavelength of optical wave inside glass medium

questiontext.text: A light wave of frequency \(\nu = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\) enters a non-magnetic glass medium with relative permittivity \(\varepsilon_r = 4.0\). What is the wavelength of the light wave inside the glass? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Frequency: \(\nu = 5.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\).
Relative permittivity: \(\varepsilon_r = 4.0\).
Relative permeability: \(\mu_r = 1.0\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Frequency of a wave remains invariant across media boundaries. The velocity in the medium is \(v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}}\), and the wavelength in the medium is \(\lambda' = \frac{v}{\nu}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[v = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\varepsilon_r}}\]\[\lambda' = \frac{v}{\nu}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate speed \(v\):
\[v = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{\sqrt{4.0}} = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{2.0} = 1.5 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\]
Calculate wavelength \(\lambda'\):
\[\lambda' = \frac{1.5 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{5.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ s}^{-1}} = 3.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m} = 300\text{ nm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Wavelength in vacuum was \(600\text{ nm}\); in a medium of refractive index \(n = 2\), it halves to \(300\text{ nm}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The wavelength of the wave inside the glass is \(300\text{ nm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q17 - Wavelength determination from harmonic wave equation

questiontext.text: The magnetic field component of a plane electromagnetic wave is given by \(B_y = (2.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}) \sin(0.5 \times 10^3 x + 1.5 \times 10^{11} t)\), where \(x\) is in metres and \(t\) in seconds. What is the wavelength \(\lambda\) of the wave? (Use \(\pi = 3.1416\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Harmonic magnetic field: \(B_y = B_0 \sin(k x + \omega t)\).
Propagation wave number: \(k = 0.5 \times 10^3\text{ rad/m} = 500\text{ rad/m}\).
Constant: \(\pi = 3.1416\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Comparing with the standard sinusoidal wave equation, the wave number is \(k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{k}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\lambda = \frac{2 \times 3.1416}{500\text{ m}^{-1}} = \frac{6.2832}{500} = 0.01257\text{ m} = 1.26\text{ cm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The wavelength of the wave is \(1.26\text{ cm}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The wavelength of the wave is \(1.26\text{ cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q18 - Frequency evaluation from harmonic angular frequency

questiontext.text: In a plane electromagnetic wave, the magnetic field is given by \(B_y = (2.0 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}) \sin(0.5 \times 10^3 x + 1.5 \times 10^{11} t)\). What is the frequency \(\nu\) of this wave? (Use \(\pi = 3.1416\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Wave equation: \(B_y = B_0 \sin(k x + \omega t)\).
Angular frequency: \(\omega = 1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ rad/s}\).
Constant: \(\pi = 3.1416\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The relationship between linear frequency and angular frequency is \(\omega = 2\pi \nu\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\nu = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[\nu = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{11}\text{ rad/s}}{2 \times 3.1416} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{11}}{6.2832} \approx 2.39 \times 10^{10}\text{ Hz} = 23.9\text{ GHz}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Checking speed: \(v = \frac{\omega}{k} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{11}}{500} = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s} = c\). The frequency is \(23.9\text{ GHz}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The frequency of the wave is \(23.9\text{ GHz}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q19 - Displacement current in alternating current capacitor circuit

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance \(C = 200\text{ pF}\) is connected across a \(220\text{ V}\) (rms), \(50\text{ Hz}\) alternating voltage supply. What is the rms value of the displacement current between the capacitor plates? (Use \(\pi = 3.142\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance: \(C = 200\text{ pF} = 200 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F} = 2.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ F}\).
RMS voltage: \(V_{\text{rms}} = 220\text{ V}\).
Frequency: \(\nu = 50\text{ Hz}\).
Constant: \(\pi = 3.142\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
In an AC circuit with a capacitor, the displacement current across the plates equals the conduction current in the external leads: \(I_{\text{rms}} = \frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{X_C} = V_{\text{rms}} (2\pi \nu C)\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[I_{\text{rms}} = 2\pi \nu C V_{\text{rms}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[I_{\text{rms}} = 2 \times 3.142 \times 50\text{ s}^{-1} \times (2.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ F}) \times 220\text{ V}\]
\[I_{\text{rms}} = 314.2 \times 4.4 \times 10^{-8}\text{ A} \approx 1.38 \times 10^{-5}\text{ A} = 13.8\,\mu\text{A}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{s}^{-1} \times \text{F} \times \text{V} = \text{A}\). The rms displacement current is \(13.8\,\mu\text{A}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The rms displacement current is \(13.8\,\mu\text{A}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q20 - Intensity of electromagnetic plane wave

questiontext.text: A plane electromagnetic wave travelling in free space has an electric field amplitude \(E_0 = 60\text{ V/m}\). What is the time-averaged intensity \(I\) of this wave? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Electric field amplitude: \(E_0 = 60\text{ V/m}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
Permittivity of free space: \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The intensity \(I\) is the time-averaged energy transmitted per unit area per unit time, given by \(I = u_{\text{avg}} c\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[I = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 c E_0^2\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[E_0^2 = (60)^2 = 3600\text{ V}^2/\text{m}^2\]
\[I = \frac{1}{2} \times (8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}) \times (3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}) \times 3600\]
\[I = 0.5 \times 2.655 \times 10^{-3} \times 3600 = 1.3275 \times 10^{-3} \times 3600 \approx 4.78\text{ W/m}^2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{W/m}^2\). The average intensity is \(4.78\text{ W/m}^2\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The time-averaged intensity of the wave is \(4.78\text{ W/m}^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q21 - RMS electric field from incident solar irradiance

questiontext.text: Solar radiation outside the Earth's atmosphere has an average intensity of \(I = 1330\text{ W/m}^2\). Treating sunlight as a plane electromagnetic wave, what is the root-mean-square value of the electric field \(E_{\text{rms}}\)? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radiation intensity: \(I = 1330\text{ W/m}^2\).
Speed of light: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
Permittivity: \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Intensity is related to the rms electric field by \(I = \varepsilon_0 c E_{\text{rms}}^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{I}{\varepsilon_0 c}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the product \(\varepsilon_0 c\):
\[\varepsilon_0 c = (8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}) \times (3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}) = 2.655 \times 10^{-3}\text{ A/V}\]
Calculate \(E_{\text{rms}}^2\):
\[E_{\text{rms}}^2 = \frac{1330}{2.655 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 5.009 \times 10^5\text{ V}^2/\text{m}^2\]
Take the square root:
\[E_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{5.009 \times 10^5} \approx 708\text{ V/m}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{V/m}\). The rms electric field is \(708\text{ V/m}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The root-mean-square electric field is \(708\text{ V/m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q22 - Total average energy density from magnetic amplitude

questiontext.text: A plane electromagnetic wave travelling in free space has a magnetic field amplitude of \(B_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T}\). What is the total average energy density \(u_{\text{avg}}\) of this wave? (Take \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\) and \(\pi = 3.142\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Magnetic field amplitude: \(B_0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T}\).
Permeability of free space: \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
In an electromagnetic wave in vacuum, electric and magnetic energy densities are equal: \(u_E = u_B = \frac{1}{4\mu_0} B_0^2\). The total average energy density is \(u_{\text{avg}} = u_E + u_B = \frac{1}{2\mu_0} B_0^2\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[u_{\text{avg}} = \frac{B_0^2}{2\mu_0}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[B_0^2 = (1.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T})^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ T}^2\]
\[2\mu_0 = 2 \\times 4 \\times 3.142 \\times 10^{-7} = 2.513 \\times 10^{-6}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\]
\[u_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-12}}{2.513 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 3.98 \times 10^{-7}\text{ J/m}^3\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{J/m}^3\). The total average energy density is \(3.98 \times 10^{-7}\text{ J/m}^3\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The total average energy density is \(3.98 \times 10^{-7}\text{ J/m}^3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q23 - Photon quantum energy of visible yellow light

questiontext.text: Using the photon relation \(E = h\nu\), what is the energy of a photon of yellow light having a frequency of \(\nu = 6.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\) in units of electron-volts (eV)? (Take Planck's constant \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\) and elementary charge \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Frequency: \(\nu = 6.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ Hz}\).
Planck's constant: \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\).
Elementary charge: \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
A single photon carries energy \(E = h\nu\). To convert joules to electron-volts, divide by \(e\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E(\text{eV}) = \frac{h\nu}{e}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate energy in Joules:
\[E = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}) \times (6.0 \times 10^{14}\text{ s}^{-1}) = 3.978 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}\]
Convert to electron-volts:
\[E(\text{eV}) = \frac{3.978 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J/eV}} \approx 2.49\text{ eV}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Visible light photons typically possess energies between \(1.8\text{ eV}\) and \(3.1\text{ eV}\). The energy of \(2.49\text{ eV}\) is correct.

Final Conceptual Answer:
The energy of the yellow light photon is \(2.49\text{ eV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q24 - Photon energy of diagnostic diagnostic X ray beam

questiontext.text: What is the photon energy in kiloelectron-volts (keV) of an X-ray having a wavelength of \(\lambda = 0.10\text{ nm}\)? (Take \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\), \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\), and \(1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Wavelength: \(\lambda = 0.10\text{ nm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}\).
Planck's constant: \(h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}\).
Speed of light: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
Elementary charge: \(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J/eV}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Photon energy is related to wavelength by \(E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[E = \frac{hc}{\lambda e}\text{ eV} = \frac{hc}{1000 \lambda e}\text{ keV}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute product \(hc\):
\[hc = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (3.0 \times 10^8) = 1.989 \times 10^{-25}\text{ J}\cdot\text{m}\]
Calculate energy in Joules:
\[E = \frac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}\text{ J}\cdot\text{m}}{1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ m}} = 1.989 \times 10^{-15}\text{ J}\]
Convert to keV:
\[E = \frac{1.989 \times 10^{-15}\text{ J}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J/eV}} = 12431\text{ eV} \approx 12.4\text{ keV}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
X-rays of \(0.1\text{ nm}\) have characteristic energies of \(12.4\text{ keV}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The photon energy of the X-ray is \(12.4\text{ keV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q25 - Ratio of wavelengths of amplitude to frequency modulation

questiontext.text: An AM radio station broadcasts at \(\nu_1 = 1000\text{ kHz}\) and an FM radio station broadcasts at \(\nu_2 = 100\text{ MHz}\). What is the ratio of the wavelength of the AM wave \(\lambda_1\) to that of the FM wave \(\lambda_2\) in free space?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
AM frequency: \( u_1 = 1000 ext{ kHz} = 1.0 imes 10^6 ext{ Hz}\).
FM frequency: \( u_2 = 100 ext{ MHz} = 1.0 imes 10^8 ext{ Hz}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
Both radio signals travel through free space at the constant speed \(c\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\lambda_1 = rac{c}{ u_1}, \quad \lambda_2 = rac{c}{ u_2} \implies rac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = rac{ u_2}{ u_1}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[ rac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2} = rac{1.0 imes 10^8 ext{ Hz}}{1.0 imes 10^6 ext{ Hz}} = 100\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
\(\lambda_1 = 300 ext{ m}\) and \(\lambda_2 = 3 ext{ m}\), confirming a ratio of \(100\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The ratio of the wavelengths is 100.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q26 - Capacitance calculation for large circular plates

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor is constructed from two circular plates each of radius \(R = 12.0\text{ cm}\) separated by a distance \(d = 5.0\text{ cm}\) in air. What is the capacitance \(C\) of this capacitor? (Take \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\) and \(\pi = 3.142\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Plate radius: \(R = 12.0\text{ cm} = 0.120\text{ m}\).
Plate separation: \(d = 5.0\text{ cm} = 0.050\text{ m}\).
Permittivity: \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}\).
Constant: \(\pi = 3.142\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor in air (neglecting fringe fields) is proportional to the plate area and inversely proportional to separation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[A = \pi R^2\]\[C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \frac{\varepsilon_0 \pi R^2}{d}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate plate area \(A\):
\[A = 3.142 \times (0.120\text{ m})^2 = 3.142 \times 0.0144\text{ m}^2 \approx 0.04524\text{ m}^2\]
Calculate capacitance \(C\):
\[C = \frac{(8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}) \times 0.04524\text{ m}^2}{0.050\text{ m}} = \frac{4.004 \times 10^{-13}}{0.050}\text{ F} \approx 8.01 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F} = 8.01\text{ pF}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{Farads (F)}\). The computed capacitance is \(8.01\text{ pF}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The capacitance of the capacitor is \(8.01\text{ pF}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q27 - Potential rate of change under constant charging

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor having circular plates of radius \(R = 12.0\text{ cm}\) and separation \(d = 5.0\text{ cm}\) (capacitance \(C = 8.01\text{ pF}\)) is charged by a constant external current of \(i = 0.15\text{ A}\). What is the time rate of change of potential difference \(\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}\) between the plates?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Capacitance: \(C = 8.01\text{ pF} = 8.01 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F}\).
Charging current: \(i = 0.15\text{ A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
For a capacitor with fixed geometry, \(Q = C V\). Differentiating with respect to time gives \(i = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}t} = C \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{i}{C}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{0.15\text{ A}}{8.01 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F}} = \frac{0.15}{8.01} \times 10^{12}\text{ V/s} \approx 1.87 \times 10^{10}\text{ V/s}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{V/s}\). The rate of potential change is \(1.87 \times 10^{10}\text{ V/s}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The rate of change of potential difference is \(1.87 \times 10^{10}\text{ V/s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q28 - Induced magnetic field amplitude inside ac capacitor

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor made of circular plates of radius \(R = 6.0\text{ cm}\) has capacitance \(C = 100\text{ pF}\). It is connected to a \(230\text{ V}\) (rms) alternating supply with angular frequency \(\omega = 300\text{ rad/s}\). What is the amplitude of the induced magnetic field \(B_0\) at a radial distance \(r = 2.0\text{ cm}\) from the central axis between the plates? (Take \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Plate radius: \(R = 6.0\text{ cm} = 0.060\text{ m}\).
Capacitance: \(C = 100\text{ pF} = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ F}\).
RMS voltage: \(V_{\text{rms}} = 230\text{ V}\).
Angular frequency: \(\omega = 300\text{ rad/s}\).
Radial distance: \(r = 2.0\text{ cm} = 0.020\text{ m} = \frac{R}{3}\).

Step 2: Conduction and Displacement Current Peaks
The peak voltage is \(V_0 = \sqrt{2} V_{\text{rms}}\).
The peak charging current is \(I_0 = \omega C V_0 = \sqrt{2} \omega C V_{\text{rms}}\):
\[I_0 = 1.4142 \times (300\text{ rad/s}) \times (1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ F}) \times 230\text{ V} \approx 9.76 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A}\]

Step 3: Magnetic Field Inside Capacitor Formula
For \(r < R\), the induced magnetic field amplitude is:
\[B_0(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I_0 r}{2\pi R^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I_0 (R/3)}{2\pi R^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I_0}{6\pi R}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[B_0 = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}) \times (9.76 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A})}{6\pi \times 0.060\text{ m}} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 9.76 \times 10^{-6}}{3 \times 0.060}\]
\[B_0 = \frac{1.952 \times 10^{-12}}{0.180} \approx 1.08 \times 10^{-11}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The induced magnetic field amplitude at \(r = 2.0\text{ cm}\) is \(1.08 \times 10^{-11}\text{ T}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The amplitude of the induced magnetic field is \(1.08 \times 10^{-11}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q29 - Induced magnetic field outside capacitor plate radius

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor made of circular plates of radius \(R = 6.0\text{ cm}\) has capacitance \(C = 100\text{ pF}\) and is connected to a \(230\text{ V}\) (rms), \(\omega = 300\text{ rad/s}\) supply (peak charging current \(I_0 = 9.76\,\mu\text{A}\)). What is the amplitude of the induced magnetic field \(B_0\) at a radial distance \(r = 12.0\text{ cm}\) from the central axis between the planes of the plates? (Take \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Plate radius: \(R = 6.0\text{ cm} = 0.060\text{ m}\).
Radial distance: \(r = 12.0\text{ cm} = 0.120\text{ m} = 2R\) (outside the plate radius).
Peak charging current: \(I_0 = 9.76 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
For \(r \ge R\), an Amperian loop of radius \(r\) encloses the entire displacement current \(I_0\). By the Ampere-Maxwell law, \(\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = B_0 (2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[B_0(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I_0}{2\pi r}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[B_0 = \frac{(4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}) \times (9.76 \times 10^{-6}\text{ A})}{2\pi \times 0.120\text{ m}} = \frac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 9.76 \times 10^{-6}}{0.120}\]
\[B_0 = \frac{1.952 \times 10^{-12}}{0.120} \approx 1.63 \times 10^{-11}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Outside the plates, the field falls off as \(\frac{1}{r}\). At \(r = 12.0\text{ cm}\), the field amplitude is \(1.63 \times 10^{-11}\text{ T}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The amplitude of the magnetic field outside the plates is \(1.63 \times 10^{-11}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q30 - Induced magnetic field from electric field rate

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor with circular plates of radius \(R = 10.0\text{ cm}\) is charging such that the electric field between the plates increases uniformly at a rate of \(\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = 1.0 \times 10^{12}\text{ V}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s})\). What is the magnitude of the induced magnetic field \(B\) at a distance \(r = 5.0\text{ cm}\) from the central axis? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Plate radius: \(R = 10.0\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}\).
Radial distance from axis: \(r = 5.0\text{ cm} = 0.050\text{ m} < R\).
Rate of electric field change: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = 1.0 \times 10^{12}\text{ V}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s})\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
For a circular path of radius \(r < R\) inside the plates, the electric flux is \(\Phi_E = E (\pi r^2)\).
Applying the Ampere-Maxwell law with \(i_c = 0\):
\[\oint \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{l} = B (2\pi r) = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi_E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 (\pi r^2) \frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t}\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[B = \frac{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0 r}{2} \frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{r}{2 c^2} \frac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[c^2 = (3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s})^2 = 9.0 \times 10^{16}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2\]
\[B = \frac{0.050\text{ m}}{2 \times (9.0 \times 10^{16}\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2)} \times (1.0 \times 10^{12}\text{ V}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s}))\]
\[B = \frac{0.050 \times 10^{12}}{1.8 \times 10^{17}} = \frac{5.0 \times 10^{10}}{1.8 \times 10^{17}} \approx 2.78 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\frac{\text{m} \cdot \text{V}/(\text{m}\cdot\text{s})}{\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2} = \frac{\text{V}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{m}^2} = \text{T}\). The induced magnetic field is \(2.78 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The magnitude of the induced magnetic field is \(2.78 \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q31 - Poynting power flux entering charging capacitor

questiontext.text: A parallel plate capacitor with circular plates of radius \(R\) and separation \(d\) is charged by a current \(i = 0.20\text{ A}\). At a certain instant, the potential difference between the plates is \(V = 100\text{ V}\). What is the instantaneous rate at which electromagnetic energy flows radially into the space between the capacitor plates across its cylindrical boundary?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Instantaneous voltage: \(V = 100\text{ V}\).
Charging current: \(i = 0.20\text{ A}\).
Plate radius: \(R\), plate separation: \(d\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The electric field is \(E = \frac{V}{d}\) (perpendicular to plates). The induced magnetic field at the cylindrical boundary (\(r = R\)) is tangential with magnitude \(B = \frac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi R}\).
The Poynting vector \(\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})\) points radially inwards toward the capacitor axis.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[S = \frac{1}{\mu_0} E B = \frac{1}{\mu_0} \left(\frac{V}{d}\right) \left(\frac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi R}\right) = \frac{V i}{2\pi R d}\]
The total power entering through the cylindrical edge area \(A_{\text{cyl}} = 2\pi R d\) is:
\[P = S \times (2\pi R d) = \left(\frac{V i}{2\pi R d}\right) (2\pi R d) = V i\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[P = 100\text{ V} \times 0.20\text{ A} = 20.0\text{ W}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Energy conservation dictates that the power entering via electromagnetic field flux equals the rate of increase of stored electrostatic energy: \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{2} C V^2\right) = V C \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = V i = 20.0\text{ W}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The rate at which electromagnetic energy flows into the capacitor is \(20.0\text{ W}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q32 - Total field energy within cubical spatial volume

questiontext.text: A plane electromagnetic wave with electric field amplitude \(E_0 = 150\text{ V/m}\) propagates in free space. What is the total time-averaged electromagnetic energy contained within a cubical volume of side length \(L = 2.0\text{ m}\)? (Take \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Electric field amplitude: \(E_0 = 150\text{ V/m}\).
Side length of cube: \(L = 2.0\text{ m}\).
Permittivity of free space: \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The total average energy density of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is \(u_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E_0^2\).
The total energy in volume \(V_{\text{box}}\) is \(U = u_{\text{avg}} V_{\text{box}}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[V_{\text{box}} = L^3\]\[u_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E_0^2\]\[U = u_{\text{avg}} L^3\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the volume:
\[V_{\text{box}} = (2.0\text{ m})^3 = 8.0\text{ m}^3\]
Calculate \(u_{\text{avg}}\):
\[u_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2} \times (8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}) \times (150\text{ V/m})^2\]
\[u_{\text{avg}} = 0.5 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 22500 \approx 9.956 \times 10^{-8}\text{ J/m}^3\]
Calculate total energy \(U\):
\[U = (9.956 \times 10^{-8}\text{ J/m}^3) \times 8.0\text{ m}^3 \approx 7.96 \times 10^{-7}\text{ J}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{J}\). The total time-averaged energy is \(7.96 \times 10^{-7}\text{ J}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The total time-averaged energy contained within the volume is \(7.96 \times 10^{-7}\text{ J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q33 - Radiation force exerted on absorbing surface

questiontext.text: A continuous laser beam with an operating power of \(P = 30\text{ mW}\) is directed normally onto a completely absorbing flat target in vacuum. What is the radiation force exerted by the beam on the target? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Beam power: \(P = 30\text{ mW} = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ W}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
The target is completely absorbing (absorption coefficient = 1).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
An electromagnetic wave carrying radiant energy \(U\) also transports linear momentum \(p = \frac{U}{c}\).
When energy is delivered at rate \(P = \frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t}\) and completely absorbed, the rate of momentum transfer is the force \(F\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[F = \frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{1}{c} \frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{P}{c}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[F = \frac{3.0 \times 10^{-2}\text{ W}}{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ N}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{W}/(\text{m/s}) = (\text{J/s})/(\text{m/s}) = \text{N}\). The force exerted is \(1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ N}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The radiation force exerted on the target is \(1.0 \times 10^{-10}\text{ N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q34 - Average energy density of elliptically polarized wave

questiontext.text: In a plane electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum along the \(z\)-axis, the electric field is given by \(\mathbf{E} = [30\sin(kz - \omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + 40\cos(kz - \omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf{j}}]\text{ V/m}\). What is the total time-averaged energy density \(u_{\text{avg}}\) of this wave? (Take \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ C}^2\text{N}^{-1}\text{m}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Electric field components: \(E_x = 30\sin(kz - \omega t)\text{ V/m}\), \(E_y = 40\cos(kz - \omega t)\text{ V/m}\).
Permittivity of free space: \(\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The square of the electric field magnitude is:
\[E^2 = E_x^2 + E_y^2 = 900\sin^2(kz - \omega t) + 1600\cos^2(kz - \omega t)\]
Since the time average of both \(\sin^2\) and \(\cos^2\) over a complete period is \(\frac{1}{2}\), the average of \(E^2\) is:
\[\langle E^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{2}(900) + \frac{1}{2}(1600) = 450 + 800 = 1250\text{ V}^2/\text{m}^2\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
The total average energy density is \(u_{\text{avg}} = \varepsilon_0 \langle E^2 \rangle\) (accounting for both electric and magnetic field contributions equally).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
\[u_{\text{avg}} = (8.85 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}) \times 1250\text{ V}^2/\text{m}^2\]
\[u_{\text{avg}} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 1250 = 1.106 \times 10^{-8}\text{ J/m}^3\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{J/m}^3\). The total average energy density is \(1.11 \times 10^{-8}\text{ J/m}^3\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The total time-averaged energy density is \(1.11 \times 10^{-8}\text{ J/m}^3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q35 - Node spacing in domestic microwave cavity

questiontext.text: A domestic microwave oven operates at a magnetron frequency of \(\nu = 2.45\text{ GHz}\). In the standing wave pattern formed inside the oven cavity, what is the distance between two adjacent electric field nodes? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Operating frequency: \(\nu = 2.45\text{ GHz} = 2.45 \times 10^9\text{ Hz}\).
Speed of light in vacuum: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
First find the wavelength \(\lambda\) of the microwaves. Inside a standing wave cavity formed by reflective metal walls, the separation between adjacent nodes is equal to half a wavelength (\(\frac{\lambda}{2}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}\]\[d_{\text{node}} = \frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{c}{2\nu}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate wavelength \(\lambda\):
\[\lambda = \frac{3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}}{2.45 \times 10^9\text{ s}^{-1}} \approx 0.1224\text{ m} = 12.24\text{ cm}\]
Calculate node spacing:
\[d_{\text{node}} = \frac{12.24\text{ cm}}{2} = 6.12\text{ cm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Units: \(\text{cm}\). The distance between adjacent nodes is approximately \(6.1\text{ cm}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The distance between adjacent electric field nodes is \(6.1\text{ cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_ELECTROMAGNETIC_WAVES_MCQ_Q36 - Peak magnetic field from solar irradiance flux

questiontext.text: Sunlight incident perpendicularly on the upper atmosphere has an average intensity of \(I = 1380\text{ W/m}^2\). Modelling sunlight as a harmonic plane electromagnetic wave, what is the peak amplitude of the magnetic field \(B_0\)? (Take \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\) and \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Average intensity: \(I = 1380\text{ W/m}^2\).
Speed of light: \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\).
Permeability of free space: \(\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
The intensity of a plane electromagnetic wave can be expressed in terms of the magnetic field amplitude \(B_0\) as:
\[I = u_{\text{avg}} c = \left(\frac{B_0^2}{2\mu_0}\right) c = \frac{c B_0^2}{2\mu_0}\]

Step 3: Relevant Formulae
\[B_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2\mu_0 I}{c}}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the numerator:
\[2\mu_0 I = 2 \times (4\pi \times 10^{-7}) \times 1380 = 8\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1380 \approx 25.1327 \times 10^{-7} \times 1380 \approx 3.468 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}^2\text{m}^2/\text{s}\]
Divide by \(c\):
\[B_0^2 = \frac{3.468 \times 10^{-3}}{3.0 \times 10^8} = 1.156 \times 10^{-11}\text{ T}^2\]
Take the square root:
\[B_0 = \sqrt{1.156 \times 10^{-11}} = \sqrt{11.56 \times 10^{-12}} = 3.40 \times 10^{-6}\text{ T} = 3.40\,\mu\text{T}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Verify with \(E_0 = c B_0 = 3.0 \times 10^8 \times 3.40 \times 10^{-6} = 1020\text{ V/m}\), and \(I = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 c E_0^2 = 0.5 \times 2.655 \times 10^{-3} \times (1020)^2 = 1380\text{ W/m}^2\). The result is \(3.40\,\mu\text{T}\).

Final Conceptual Answer:
The peak amplitude of the magnetic field is \(3.40\,\mu\text{T}\).
